profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Lowest eval speedup in the round (0.1996, 43.7 us vs 8.7 us reference) and the representative of the untouched legacy all-reduce path on a contiguous 1D full reduction.

Control workload: smallest shape (64x64, best speedup 1.872) exercising the same amin_last_kernel with a single program, used to falsify 'the last-axis kernel is inherently slow' and isolate the ::2 regression to tile geometry.
Sharpest regression of the round versus round 1 (0.5691 -> 0.2633 speedup; latency 0.0402 -> 0.0867 ms) on the 4096x4096 last-axis shape; boundary between the improved ::1 and ::4 regimes.
Largest absolute win of the round (+349% vs round 1, 10.97 -> 2.44 ms) and representative of the new copy-free middle-axis amin_mid_kernel on the 2.1 GB fp16 1024^3 shape.
Highest eval latency of the round (3.331 ms) and the fp32 counterexample to the fp16 1024^3 regime, testing whether the middle-axis kernel is memory- or vector-bound by dtype.

findings.label: 1D full reduction runs the legacy two-launch path: AIV is 63% MTE3 / 25% scalar / 5% vector over 1024 tiny programs
findings.backend_detail: Ascend AIV pipes: aiv_mte3_ratio 0.63, aiv_scalar_ratio 0.25, aiv_vec_ratio 0.05, cube_utilization 0 (no cube use); 1024 blocks, 100 measured invocations; two kernels per call.

evidence.value: amin_kernel_1 + amin_kernel_2 (legacy all-reduce pair; no amin_split_kernel present)

findings.inference: For [1048576] the host still takes the legacy full-reduction path: two launches (46.45 us + 1.24 us per call) over 1024 single-row programs of ~1024 fp16 elements each. The AIV busy profile (MTE3 0.63, scalar 0.25, vector 0.05 out of 45.1 us) shows the kernel does almost no vector work and spends its time in UB-to-GM write-back of per-program partials plus scalar bookkeeping, so adding vector width or unrolling inside this structure cannot help much; the win must come from using far fewer, much larger programs whose partials are combined by the already-written two-stage split kernels. This is the lowest-speedup workload of the round (0.1996, ref 8.72 us vs 43.67 us) and it did not change in this round (latency -1.7%, within noise), consistent with the plan keeping the legacy all-reduce path untouched.

findings.label: fp16 1024^3 middle-axis kernel: MTE2 (1.61 TB/s stream) and vector are nearly serialized, kernel time ~= vec + MTE2
findings.backend_detail: Ascend AIV: aiv_vec_ratio 0.557, aiv_mte2_ratio 0.545, aiv_scalar_ratio 0.113, aiv_mte3_ratio 0.002, cube_utilization 0; 1024 blocks; single kernel per call (copy-free, no dim_compress).
findings.inference: The kernel moves 2.147 GB of fp16 input in 1332 us of MTE2 busy time (~1.61 TB/s, consistent with a near-peak streaming read), while the vector pipe is busy 1362 us for the 1.07 G min operations. Kernel wall time (2446 us) is approximately the SUM of the two pipes rather than their maximum, i.e. load and compute are essentially serialized: the observed non-overlap costs ~1.08 ms per call. Both pipes are individually near their own limit, so this workload is memory-bandwidth bound and the remaining headroom is pipelining (double-buffered tiles / more in-flight MTE2), with a theoretical floor near the reference's 1.418 ms vs the current 2.440 ms (eval speedup 0.581).

findings.label: fp32 1024^3 middle-axis kernel is vector-pipe bound (vec 0.70 vs MTE2 0.49)
findings.backend_detail: Ascend AIV: aiv_vec_ratio 0.701, aiv_mte2_ratio 0.491, aiv_scalar_ratio 0.080, cube_utilization 0; 1024 blocks.
findings.inference: For fp32 the same mid-axis kernel is vector-bound (0.70) while MTE2 is only partially overlapped (0.49); 4.29 GB of input at 1635 us MTE2 implies the load path is not the limiter here, whereas 2335 us of vector time for the 1.07 G min ops is. Since fp32 doubles both bytes and vector lanes per element, this regime needs fewer vector instructions per element (wider vectorized min, less per-element masking/scalar address math) rather than more memory parallelism. Eval speedup 0.848 (3.331 ms vs ref 2.825 ms) is already the best of the 1024^3 set.

findings.label: REGRESSION: float16 4096x4096 last-axis kernel runs 2048 two-row programs with scalar 0.34 / vec 0.46 / MTE2 0.17 (BLOCK_N capped at 2048 vs row width 4096)
findings.backend_detail: Ascend AIV: aiv_vec_ratio 0.4615, aiv_scalar_ratio 0.3369, aiv_mte2_ratio 0.1681, aiv_mte3_ratio 0.2223, cube_utilization 0; 2048 blocks, kernel 88.6 us avg (eval latency 86.7 us).

evidence.metric: per-invocation pipe times (aiv_time / vec / scalar / mte2 / mte3)

evidence.value: failed: 'profiling deadline expired during Ascend simulator kernel 0' (75 s budget exhausted; only a profile timeout log was produced)

findings.inference: 2048 blocks for 4096 rows means each program owns only 2 rows, and the host key_param last_path_BLOCK_N = min(next_pow2(N), 2048) forces two 2048-wide chunks to accumulate each 4096-wide row; the resulting per-program loop/address overhead shows up as scalar 0.34 of AIV time with vector stuck at 0.46 and MTE2 at only 0.17 (a strided 2-row tile, so wide coalesced reads are absent). Eval data for the same shape across all three dtypes regressed sharply versus round 1 (fp16 0.5691 -> 0.2633, i.e. 0.0402 -> 0.0867 ms; fp32 0.6978 -> 0.4153; bf16 0.4583 -> 0.2921) while the single-program last-axis case ::1 improved (0.8765 -> 1.8720), which points at the tile geometry rather than the kernel family. Instruction-level confirmation could not be obtained: the Ascend simulator budget expired for this kernel.

findings.label: Control: single-program last-axis kernel (64x64) beats both round-1 baseline and reference, so the last-axis kernel family is not the problem
findings.backend_detail: Ascend AIV: 1 block, aiv_time 3.867 us of a 4.4 us kernel; profiler time is diagnostic (eval latency 1.954 us).
findings.inference: The same amin_last_kernel with a full-row tile (BLOCK_N = next_pow2(64) = 64, BLOCK_M = 1, grid = 1) delivers eval speedup 1.8720 (1.954 us vs 3.658 us reference), better than both the reference and the round-1 value 0.8765. This control separates the two candidate causes of the ::2 regression: the kernel family itself is competitive, whereas the 4096-row case is executed with 2048 small programs and a 2-chunk row loop. It also shows this tiny shape is pure launch/latency overhead (8 KB of data in ~2-4 us), so it should not drive the next experiment.

performance_interpretation: Round 2 is a net win: eval geo_mean rose 0.3017 -> 0.5118 (+69.6%) at unchanged correctness (all 12 flaggems correctness workloads PASSED). The profiler confirms the frozen hypothesis for the middle-axis dim-reduction regime and for single-tile last-axis shapes: the 64x512x512 and 1024x1024x1024 timing pairs (::3, ::4) run a single copy-free kernel (amin_mid_kernel) with no dim_compress copy and no chunked relaunch, and their eval speedups jumped 2.3x-5.4x. The hypothesis is NOT confirmed for two other regimes. (a) The 1D full reduction [1048576] (::0, lowest speedup in the round, 0.1996) still executes the unchanged legacy two-launch path (amin_kernel_1 + amin_kernel_2); its AIV is 63% MTE3 (UB->GM partial write-back), 25% scalar and only 5% vector over 1024 tiny programs, i.e. it is overhead/data-movement bound and is ~5x behind the reference - the new amin_split_kernel/amin_split_final_kernel pair is never dispatched for this contiguous full-reduction case. (b) The 4096x4096 last-axis reduction (::2) REGRESSED on all three dtypes relative to round 1 (fp16 0.5691->0.2633, fp32 0.6978->0.4153, bf16 0.4583->0.2921); the profile of float16::2 shows 2048 programs each covering only 2 rows with vec 0.46 / scalar 0.34 / MTE2 0.17, which is consistent with the host BLOCK_N cap of 2048 forcing a two-chunk loop over each 4096-wide row plus a strided 2-row tile, so per-program overhead - not a copy - is now the limit. Net conclusion: copy removal was the right lever where a copy actually existed (::3/::4) and for single-tile shapes (::1, +113%), but the remaining gap in this round is no longer a copy problem; it splits into (i) a full-reduction dispatch that bypasses the new split kernels and (ii) an under-sized last-axis tile for wide rows. Profiler timing is diagnostic and does not replace eval latency (e.g. float16::1 profiled at 2.34-4.64 us vs 1.954 us eval).

next_experiment.action_description: Extend the copy-free single-dimension fast path to contiguous FULL reductions: when the reduced set covers the entire contiguous tensor (e.g. 1D [N], or dim over every axis, viewed as (1, N)) and N >= 65536, dispatch the already-written two-stage split reduction (amin_split_kernel with S = min(1024, cdiv(N, 16384)) followed by amin_split_final_kernel) instead of the legacy amin_kernel_1 + amin_kernel_2 all-reduce pair. Keep the legacy all-reduce path for non-contiguous, multi-axis and small-N inputs. Do not change any kernel math, and leave the dim_compress fallback untouched.
next_experiment.expected_impact: The three 1D workloads (float16/float32/bfloat16 ::0) are the round's lowest-speedup cases (0.1996 / 0.2246 / 0.1911) and their profiled 1D kernel is 63% MTE3 + 25% scalar with only 5% vector over 1024 tiny programs; replacing 1024 small partial programs plus 2 launches with S=64 larger split programs plus one final kernel should cut the 43.7/39.6/44.2 us latencies substantially (reference is 8.7/8.9/8.4 us). A 2.5x improvement on just these three workloads raises the headline geo_mean from 0.5118 to about 0.63 without touching the already-winning ::3/::4 paths.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risks: tail masking when N is not a multiple of the split tile, keepdim/output-shape regressions for the reduced case, extra launch overhead if the N>=65536 guard is set too low (small 1D tensors such as [1024] are correctly served by the current path), and the split final kernel's dtype handling (fp32 accumulator) for fp16/bf16 stores. Rollback is a one-line dispatch revert to the legacy all-reduce call; no kernel code needs to be undone. Validate correctness on the 12 flaggems amin cases before timing.
success_criteria: All 12 flaggems correctness workloads still PASSED for the new candidate (no output-shape or keepdim mismatch).
Each of float16/float32/bfloat16 ::0 improves its eval speedup by at least 2x versus round 2 (i.e. >= 0.40 / 0.45 / 0.38) with latency <= 22 us / 20 us / 22 us.
No other timing workload regresses more than 5% versus round 2, in particular ::2 (which already regressed) and ::3/::4.
Headline evaluation geo_mean increases above the round-2 value 0.5118 (target >= 0.58).

warnings: Instruction-level (simulator) profiling of amin_last_kernel for float16::2 was attempted and FAILED with 'profiling deadline expired during Ascend simulator kernel 0' (75 s budget); only a profile timeout log and a kernel-discovery log were produced, so no SASS-like instruction listing backs the ::2 diagnosis.
msprof timings are diagnostic only and do not replace eval latency (e.g. float16::1 profiled at 2.34 us avg while eval reports 1.954 ms/us); no eval number in this analysis comes from the profiler.

Only 5 of the 15 timing workloads were profiled; the ::2 regression is confirmed by profiler evidence for float16 only, while the fp32/bfloat16 ::2 regressions are inferred from the frozen eval comparison, and no ::3 or bfloat16 ::4 workload was profiled.
open_questions: The 4096x4096 last-axis regression (::2) is a real remaining defect but is deliberately not the recommended next experiment: the host caps last_path_BLOCK_N at 2048 for a 4096-wide row and forces 2048 two-row programs. A follow-up should raise the cap (BLOCK_N = next_pow2(N), BLOCK_M = 1 full-row tiles) and re-measure, since ::1 shows the same kernel wins when the tile spans the full row.

The fp16 1024^3 middle-axis kernel shows vec (1362 us) and MTE2 (1332 us) nearly additive, so whether a pipelined (double-buffered) mid-axis loop can approach the 1.4 ms reference floor is unresolved and should be tested separately from the dispatch experiment.

The 1D amin_kernel_1 output shape is a 1024-element tensor while AIV MTE3 dominates 63% of busy time, so the exact partial-combination mechanism could not be confirmed without instruction-level evidence; the recommendation only relies on the measured pipe ratios and program count.
